title: Rare events
description: 2000 particles from the stationary law of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process $dX_t = -X_t\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t$ (σ = 1), so $X^1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \frac12)$. The Observable is the indicator $\mathbf{1}_{x_1 > 2}$: its mean estimates the small probability $p = P(X^1 > 2)$, and the dashed line is the exact value. For a rare event the relative error of plain Monte Carlo is $\sqrt{(1 - p)/(Np)}$, which is why importance sampling simulates a biased SDE $dY = (a + b\alpha)\,dt + b\,dW$ and reweights every path with the Girsanov weight $w = \exp(-\frac12\int|\alpha|^2 dt - \int\alpha\,dW)$ (course notes, §5.1.4.4 and §5.2.4.2).

questions.text: About how many of the 2000 particles are in the event at any moment?
Relative standard error $\sqrt{(1-p)/(Np)}$ of the estimate with N = 2000?
How many particles would plain Monte Carlo need for a relative error of 10 %?
Watch the estimate jump. Why is the confidence interval of the window misleading here (look at how it is computed from few nonzero values)?
Importance sampling: which constant bias drift α would you choose so that about half of the biased particles end up beyond $x_1 = 2$? What happens to the weights if α is much too large?
With the GPU (Settings shows the integrator) you can simulate 50 000 particles. Add them with the Particles tool and compare the estimate with the exact value.
